# Summary {#part-orientation-summary .unnumbered}

The opening part followed one request across the layers of the stack, then pulled back to mark which claims are settled enough to build on and which are still disputed. It sorted the vocabulary the field borrows from neighboring disciplines into borrowed mechanisms and borrowed pictures, because a useful metaphor read too literally gives a false account of the mechanism. And it drew the subject's boundary: the generative lifecycle this book covers sits beside the ranking and recommendation infrastructure that already ran feeds, search, and ad auctions, inheriting its retrieval funnels and measurement discipline while needing a serving tier of its own.

Local symptoms often have non-local causes. A benchmark jump, a latency incident, a large GPU bill, or an agent failure may be decided by a layer the symptom does not name. The part introduced the constraint arrow to mark such cases: a design choice that looks arbitrary in one layer is often dictated by a cost paid in the layer below.

What remains open is how to update the map as the field changes without reducing it to a list of recent releases. Some disputed claims will become settled engineering practice; others will remain provisional longer than their usual confident phrasing suggests. The rest of the book uses this orientation to place each topic in the stack and to judge how settled its claims are. Part I turns that map into material choices: compute budgets, data mixtures, tokenizers, architectures, and training runs.
